extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; students of literature, philosophy, and Renaissance essays
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and extraction of normative principles and evaluative statements from Montaigne's Essays (chapters on constancy, ceremony, cowardice, ambassadors, fear, and happiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy (law of resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The law of resolution and constancy does not imply that we ought not, as much as in us lies, to decline and secure ourselves from the mischiefs and inconveniences that threaten us... the business of constancy chiefly is, bravely to stand to, and stoutly to suffer those inconveniences which are not possibly to be avoided.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constancy is not reckless stubbornness: take all decent and honest means to secure yourself from harm, but endure bravely those unavoidable misfortunes. Examples and caveats: evasive motions in combat that protect one from blows are acceptable; one should not condemn protective or ungraceful motions if they preserve life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical retreat can be virtuous
rubrics_metrics.description: “Several very warlike nations have made use of a retreating and flying way of fight as a thing of singular advantage... Socrates... laughs at Laches, who had defined fortitude to be a standing firm in the ranks against the enemy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing one’s ground is not the sole measure of courage; retreat or feigned flight can be a valid, skillful, and honorable tactic (examples: Turks, Scythians, Lacedaemonians at Plataea). Evaluate bravery contextually by strategic outcome rather than mere immobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pointless obstinacy in defense
rubrics_metrics.description: “Valour has its bounds as well as other virtues, which, once transgressed, the next step is into the territories of vice... men are justly punished for being obstinate in the defence of a fort that is not in reason to be defended.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage has limits; defending an indefensible position is folly and may rightly be punished. Judgment should weigh relative forces, reputation, and context (examples of commanders executing stubborn defenders; compare two culverins vs thirty pieces of cannon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate infirmity from malice in judging cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: “'Tis reason that a man should make a great difference betwixt faults that merely proceed from infirmity, and those that are visibly the effects of treachery and malice... many have thought we are not fairly questionable for anything but what we commit against our conscience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish acts born of natural weakness or ignorance from deliberate treachery; punishers and laws should calibrate penalties accordingly (examples: public shame used by Charondas versus death for treachery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic ideal: preserve judgment though feel passions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Stoics... consent that he should tremble at the terrible noise of thunder... provided his judgment remain sound and entire, and that the seat of his reason suffer no concussion nor alteration, and that he yield no consent to his fright and discomposure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External signs of fear or perturbation are permissible; the critical standard is whether reason and judgment remain intact. Anti-pattern: letting initial fright penetrate to and corrupt judgement and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in handling passions (Peripatetic view)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Peripatetic sage does not exempt himself totally from perturbations of mind, but he moderates them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where Stoics aim for unmoved reason, peripatetics accept feelings but counsel moderation; emotional responses should be tempered, not repressed nor indulged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward divination and prophetic vagueness
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is hardly possible but that these alleged authorities sometimes stumble upon a truth amongst an infinite number of lies... nobody records their flimflams and false prognostics... but if they chop upon one truth, that carries a mighty report.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One accurate hit amid many falsehoods does not validate the practice; be wary of ambiguous prophecies framed so posterity can interpret them to fit events (example: prophetic canting that shrouds sense in riddle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust improvisatory impulses only in well-prepared minds
rubrics_metrics.description: “Socrates demon might, perhaps, be no other but a certain impulsion of the will... in a soul so enlightened as his was, and so prepared by a continual exercise of wisdom and virtue, 'tis to be supposed those inclinations... were very important and worthy to be followed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sudden promptings or inspirations (the 'demon') can be valuable if the person's judgment has been cultivated by habitual wisdom; do not generalize their authority to the unpractised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy and good manners are necessary but not enslaving
rubrics_metrics.description: “Still, these excesses excepted, the knowledge of courtesy and good manners is a very necessary study... I love to follow them, but not to be so servilely tied to their observation that my whole life should be enslaved to ceremonies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe civility: it creates liking and opens social doors, but avoid becoming a slave to ceremony; occasional omission for discretion can be as handsome as strict observance. Examples: rules about receiving visitors, yet King Francis and others showing deference by waiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of precedence in social ceremony
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a common rule in all assemblies, that those of less quality are to be first upon the place, by reason that it is more due to the better sort to make others wait and expect them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social hierarchy often dictates protocol (e.g., who arrives first), yet exceptions and gestures of deference (greater arriving later) can signal respect; know local customs but apply with discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambassadors must report full truth to their sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: “I could not but wonder that it should be in the power of an ambassador to dispense with anything which he ought to signify to his master... either to conceal or to disguise the truth... should seem... to him who is only to receive it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diplomats owe their masters full and faithful accounts of proceedings, leaving judgment and action to the sovereign. Concealment of significant facts is a betrayal of duty (example: ambassadors hiding injurious passages from Langey's account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance obedience and discretionary judgment in delegated roles
rubrics_metrics.description: “We so willingly slip the collar of command upon any pretence... no utility whatever derived from the wit or valour of those he employs ought to be so dear to a superior as a downright and sincere obedience... Notwithstanding, we may on the other side consider that so precise and implicit an obedience as this is only due to positive and limited commands.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commanders should expect obedience to explicit orders, but agents with broad mandates (e.g., ambassadors) require discretion; excessive micromanagement (lack of rein) can harm affairs. Example: Persian kings' over-control prejudicing their dominion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from people's expertise; evaluate sources by profession
rubrics_metrics.description: “...make it his business always to put the architect, the painter, the statuary, every mechanic artisan, upon discourse of their own capacities... in reading histories... consider what kind of men are the authors... if physicians... incline to credit what they report of the temperature of the air...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek information from those expert in a subject; weigh authors' accounts by their professions and likely competence in the matters they treat. Anti-pattern: letting individuals prate beyond their competence (lawyer pontificating on mechanics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear undermines judgment and can be more oppressive than death
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am not so good a naturalist... 'tis a strange passion, and such a one that the physicians say there is no other whatever that sooner dethrones our judgment... The thing in the world I am most afraid of is fear... fear is more importunate and insupportable than death itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fear is uniquely destructive of reason and can produce mania, panic, and irrational acts; training and prior experience mitigate fear (veterans vs those newly frightened). Recognize panic phenomena (collective terror) and the need to preserve composure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not declare someone happy until after death
rubrics_metrics.description: “The very children know the story of King Croesus... That men, however fortune may smile upon them, could never be said to be happy till they had been seen to pass over the last day of their lives.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is contingent and retrospective: final judgment on a life’s happiness requires seeing its ultimate outcome because fortune is mutable. Anti-pattern: premature eulogizing of present success as definitive happiness.
